card.hook: You've puffed up through the redwoods, reached the platform, and Pōhutu is hiding in its own cloud of steam. Don't worry. The whole valley is laid out below you, and the geyser does turn up eventually.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Lower Whaka Lookout, the wooden platform on the Pohaturoa (yellow) Track in Whakarewarewa Forest. Face north-west and look down over the valley, with Pōhutu, the mud lake and the steaming vents in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the whole valley and the town beyond. Then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to bring Pōhutu and its steam closer. Use 0.5x only if you want the redwoods and the platform rail in the shot.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the steam, then drag the brightness slider down a touch so the white plume keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Pōhutu erupts roughly 20 times a day, so patience matters more than the clock. Give the steam time to clear. Early morning or late afternoon may be easier on the light, since you'll be facing north-west.
card.selfie_here: Try the geyser viewing area a short walk from Te Puia's entrance, on the platform about 50–80 m from Pōhutu. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if you have it, and keep the geyser over your shoulder. Morning light helps the steam catch the sun.
card.ask_someone: At the Lower Whaka Lookout, ask a fellow walker to take your photo while you stand at the platform rail with the valley behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Keep to the marked paths around the thermal features. The ground beside steaming vents can be unstable and hot, and the barriers are there for good reason. The lookout is free, but entry to Te Puia itself is ticketed, so check the official site first.
card.challenge: Switch on gridlines, park the steam plume on one vertical line, and see if you can click just as Pōhutu starts to rise.
card.good_to_know: Te Puia sits in the Whakarewarewa geothermal valley and is home to the New Zealand Māori Arts and Crafts Institute. The Institute grew out of a carving school founded in 1926 by Sir Āpirana Ngata, and the current Institute opened in 1963. Guided tours through the valley go back to the mid-19th century. Up close at Geyser Flat (ticket needed), the plume can rise to about 30 metres.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the Lower Whaka Lookout, the wooden platform on the Pohaturoa (yellow) Track in Whakarewarewa Forest. Face north-west and look down over the valley, with Pōhutu, the mud lake and the steaming vents in front of you.

card.hook: Steam curls off the pools, the lake sits flat and wide behind them, and a park fills the background. You get all of it in one shot, and you don't even have to get wet.
card.stand_here: Stand on the lakeside path in Government Gardens, along the Lake Rotorua shore, and face the spa complex. You'll see the spa's lakefront pool area and the lake together, with the park's historic gardens behind the shoreline.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the lake, the pools and the gardens in together. Switch to 1x for a cleaner, less stretched look, then try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the steam.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the steam, then drag the slider to make the picture a little darker so the steam doesn't turn white.
card.best_time: Go when the light is soft and the sun is low, not straight overhead. Steam shows up best against a darker background.
card.selfie_here: Try the Rachel Spring pool on Hatupatu Drive, right beside the spa. One guide recommends it for sunrise and sunset photos, and it should put the spa close behind you if you face the lake. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x, and tuck the view over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Please don't frame bathers who are in the water. If you walk the Sulphur Point boardwalk, stay on the boardwalks and marked paths, because the ground near the geothermal activity can be unsafe.
card.challenge: Take three shots a second or two apart and see which one gives the steam the best shape.
card.good_to_know: Local Māori bathed here for centuries in an acidic pool called Te Pupunitanga, now known as Priest's Bath. In 1878 Father Mahoney, a Catholic priest, bathed in hand-dug pools on this spot and found his arthritis eased. The Pavilion Bath House opened in 1882, the Ward Baths followed in 1931, and the site has been called Polynesian Spa since 1972.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the lakeside path in Government Gardens, along the Lake Rotorua shore, and face the spa complex. You'll see the spa's lakefront pool area and the lake together, with the park's historic gardens behind the shoreline.

card.hook: A giant Shaun the Sheep is waiting on the lawn at the Agrodome in Rotorua, and honestly, he's a better poser than most of us. He's the easy win here, so start with him.
card.stand_here: Stand about 430 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east. Shaun is on the lawn outside the Agrodome, so walk east towards him.
card.zoom: Use 1x for the main shot of Shaun. Switch to 0.5x if you want the whole lawn in the frame. For the farm view from the Woollen Mill Cafe area, try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the paddocks.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and put Shaun on one third of the frame, leaving the surroundings in the other two thirds.
card.best_time: Go in the daytime, when the grounds are open. The farm shows run three times a day, so that's when you'll get a busier, livelier frame.
card.selfie_here: Squeeze in beside the giant Shaun statue on the lawn near the front entrance. There's also a Shaun the Sheep photo backdrop just outside the show arena if you want a second go. Use the front camera, hold it a bit low, and keep Shaun over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand on the lawn by the Shaun statue and frame the shot so the glass-fronted visitor building fills the background, while you pose beside Shaun.
card.rules_and_safety: Stay out of the way of other visitors. Parts of the site may be ticketed, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get Shaun's face and your best sheepish grin in the same frame, then see who looks more pleased with themselves.
card.good_to_know: The Agrodome opened in 1971, founded by champion sheep shearer Godfrey Bowen and local farmer George Harford. It has been majority-owned by Ngāi Tahu Tourism since 2011. Today it keeps 26 sheep breeds, and the National Kiwi Hatchery moved into a new building here in December 2023.

card.hook: Picture a perfectly normal park, with gardens, paths and the odd bench, except the ground is steaming and the pools are bubbling. That odd mix is exactly why your photo will say "Rotorua" at a glance.
card.stand_here: Head for the west side of Pukeroa Hill, where the park is about 380 m to the south. Face south and look down over the gardens and the steaming pools.
card.zoom: Use zoom 1x to get the whole park in one go. Then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out puffs of steam and the winding paths. Once you're down among the pools, zoom 0.5x fits the steam and the paths in one frame.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on the top line so the gardens and steam fill the space below, then tap a darker part of the scene and slide it a little darker so the white steam keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Go on a day with a light breeze, because on still days steam can blanket everything. If it's hazy, wait a few minutes or move to a different angle, and take a few shots in a row so you can pick the clearest one.
card.selfie_here: Take your selfie on the wooden boardwalk over Kuirau Lake at the park's northern end, with the steaming water behind you. Use the front camera, hold it a bit low and wide, and let the steam drift into the background.
card.ask_someone: On the west side of Pukeroa Hill, ask a passer-by to stand a few steps away facing the park while you stand with the view behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Stay on the marked paths and boardwalks, keep behind any fencing, and stay well back from the edges of pools and vents, however good the shot looks. Some springs overflow onto the paths, so take it slow. The crater-lake bridge has been reported closed at times, so check when you arrive.
card.challenge: Take three shots in a row and see if you can catch the moment the breeze clears the steam and the pools show through.
card.good_to_know: Kuirau Park is a thermal park in Rotorua, with gardens and walkways among steaming, bubbling pools and vents. The ground is geothermally active, so some springs spill onto the paths. No charge is listed for the park or the hill, but check the official site before you go.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for the west side of Pukeroa Hill, where the park is about 380 m to the south. Face south and look down over the gardens and the steaming pools.

card.hook: Pōhutu Geyser doesn't perform on cue, and the waiting is half the fun. When it finally goes, it can throw a column of steam and hot water up to about 30 m, with the whole steaming valley in the same shot.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the subject, within the Whakarewarewa Thermal Reserve, in front of the geyser's viewing area. Face the geyser so the plume and the valley fit in one frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the geyser and the valley together. Then try zoom 2x-5x (depends on your phone) to fill the frame with the plume, and use zoom 0.5x only when you want the whole steaming valley and the sky.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the geyser, then slide it a little darker so the white steam keeps its detail instead of turning into a blank patch.
card.best_time: Eruptions come roughly hourly, so plan around the geyser rather than the clock and allow time for a wait. Cool, calm days show the steam best, and a dark or evenly cloudy sky behind it makes the white plume stand out.
card.selfie_here: Try the upper lookout platform inside the living Māori village, which gives a better angle on the geysers than other vantage points. Use the front camera, zoom 0.5x if you can, and keep the geyser over your shoulder. The hilltop lookout points south of the village also show the plumes in the background. Check your framing on the spot.
card.ask_someone: At the Pōhutu lookouts marked on the village map, ask a fellow visitor to take your photo with you in front and the geyser behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The valley and Pōhutu sit inside a ticketed reserve (Te Puia), so entry isn't free. Check the official site before you go, and ask a guide where photos are appropriate in the nearby village.
card.challenge: Catch the plume three times in one eruption: building, at its peak, and fading away. Bonus points if your head isn't in the way of any of them.
card.good_to_know: If the little neighbour Prince of Wales Feathers starts up, get your phone ready, because it usually plays just before Pōhutu. Māori have lived here since a fortress was first occupied around 1325, and they still use the heat of the ground for cooking and warmth. The valley holds some 500 pools and at least 65 geyser vents, though only a handful are active today.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the subject, within the Whakarewarewa Thermal Reserve, in front of the geyser's viewing area. Face the geyser so the plume and the valley fit in one frame.

card.hook: You know that feeling when you tip your head back and the trees just keep going? The Redwood Memorial Grove does that on a short, easy walk.
card.stand_here: Stand in the Redwood Memorial Grove and face the boardwalk across the thermal pond, with the long line of tall redwoods behind it. Whakarewarewa Forest is to the south of you.
card.zoom: Use zoom 0.5x in the grove to fit the full height of the redwoods in. Switch to 1x for the boardwalk and pond. At the lookouts, try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out Te Puia, the lake or Mount Ngongotaha.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the boardwalk on a diagonal so it leads into the trees, and tap the brightest part of the trees or pond, then slide it a little darker so the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: One photo guide suggests before 9 AM, when the sun glows through the trees from behind, or after 4:30 PM for softer side light.
card.selfie_here: Try the boardwalk over the old thermal pond on the Redwood Memorial Grove Track, which is a favourite with photographers. Use the front camera, hold it low, and let the redwoods tower behind your shoulder. You could also stand in the middle of Forest Avenue and look up into the trees.
card.ask_someone: At Quarry Lookout, ask a passer-by to face you while you stand at the lookout point, so the Redwood Grove and the view are spread out below you.
card.rules_and_safety: Mountain bikes share the trails, so listen for them and step aside. Keep group photos short and don't block the path. The lookouts are on forest tracks that need hiking boots and some fitness.
card.challenge: Can you get a redwood trunk from bottom to top in one shot with zoom 0.5x, with your shoes in the corner to show how huge it is?
card.good_to_know: The Redwood Memorial Grove is an easy, free walk from the visitor information centre. The redwoods here were planted, and most visitors treat the grove as the forest's main photo area. The Redwoods Treewalk is a separate paid attraction, so check the official site before you go.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in the Redwood Memorial Grove and face the boardwalk across the thermal pond, with the long line of tall redwoods behind it. Whakarewarewa Forest is to the south of you.

card.hook: From the Lower Whaka Lookout, Pōhutu looks pretty modest at first glance, like a steamy kettle far down the valley. Then the column shoots up and everyone on the platform says "ohhh" at the same time.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Lower Whaka Lookout, the wooden platform on the Pohaturoa (yellow) Track in Whakarewarewa Forest, and face north, because the geyser is to the north. You'll look down over Te Puia, the geyser, the mud lake and the steaming vents.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the whole valley, then try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to bring the geyser and its steam closer. Use zoom 0.5x only if you want the forest edge as a foreground, because the geyser will look tiny.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the geyser, then drag the slider to make the picture a little darker so the white steam keeps its detail instead of turning flat white.
card.best_time: Eruptions aren't on a timetable (anywhere from roughly hourly to about twenty a day), so plan to wait with your phone ready. For a clear view of the geyser itself, shoot once the steam has drifted off the cone.
card.selfie_here: At the Lower Whaka Lookout, use the front camera and keep the valley behind you, but expect the geyser to look small from this high up. For a bigger geyser, the raised platform southeast of Geyser Flat inside Te Puia has a better angle once the steam clears, so steam is less likely to blot out your selfie.
card.ask_someone: At the overlook just after the Te Puia admissions gate, ask a passer-by to stand a few steps back from you while you face them with Geyser Flat and Pōhutu behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Keep to the marked paths and stay out of closed areas near hot springs and mud pools. Trail access can change, so check the Whakarewarewa Forest signage before you walk, and note the closest views of Pōhutu are inside ticketed Te Puia.
card.challenge: Switch on Live Photo or burst mode and try to catch the exact moment the column starts to rise.
card.good_to_know: Pōhutu is the largest geyser in the southern hemisphere and can erupt up to about twenty times a day, sending water as high as 30 m. Its name comes from te reo Māori and is translated as 'big splash', 'explosion' or 'constant splashing'. The crater is only about 50 cm across, so the show comes from the tall column and the drifting steam.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the Lower Whaka Lookout, the wooden platform on the Pohaturoa (yellow) Track in Whakarewarewa Forest, and face north, because the geyser is to the north. You'll look down over Te Puia, the geyser, the mud lake and the steaming vents.
